| **Abstract**<br><br>Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) in factory control rooms demand the highest levels of reliability and safety. Traditional manual testing of web-based HMIs is labour-intensive, prone to human mistake, and unable to keep pace with modern agile workflows. This thesis presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of an end-to-end automated testing frame-work for web-based HMI. Leveraging Playwright for reliable browser auto-mation, Docker for environment consistency, and Bamboo/Bitbucket for continuous integration and continuous development, the framework em-beds automated tests directly into the pull-request workflow to provide im-mediate feedback on every commit.<br><br>A comparative analysis of leading test frameworks (Selenium, Cypress, Puppeteer, Nightwatch, Playwright) against project-specific criteria, demonstrated Playwright's superiority in minimizing flakiness and maxim-izing maintainability. The implemented solution executes modular end-to-end scenarios within containerized environment, generating interactive re-ports. Over 45 commit-triggered runs, the mean execution time was 275 seconds with a flakiness rate of 4.4 % (eliminated by a single retry), and 100 % pull-request gating effectiveness.<br><br>By benchmarking against ISO 9241-210 and ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015, this work establishes a human and safety centred testing baseline. The frame-work replaces manual regression testing with a reproducible, rapid feed-back mechanism, significantly reducing risk and accelerating development velocity. | | |
| **Keywords** Automated testing; end-to-end (E2E); Human-Machine Inter-face; Playwright; CI/CD; Docker; safety-critical systems; HMI testing. | | |

# Introduction

Over the past decade, testing has received increasing attention for Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) used in industrial manufacturing, where a sin-gle millisecond lag can endanger human lives and result in unplanned downtime costing millions of dollars (Ruari, n.d.) (Wang, et al., 2020).

Therefore, ensuring the performance reliability as well as usability of HMIs is a top priority. HMI testing is typically manually conducted, in which test-ers simulate operator interactions such as clicks, data entries, navigation flows, and verify that the interface responds correctly by checking graphical layouts and control commands. On the other hand, automated frameworks generally integrate with continuous integration (CI) and continuous deliv-ery (CD) pipelines to run these tests on every software update, ensuring that reliability is maintained without manual effort. Poor interface design com-bined with insufficient testing has been shown to significantly contribute to human error in industrial settings. For example, a series of operator mis-takes at Chernobyl were traced back to inadequate system feedback and de-sign shortcomings (Wang, et al., 2020).

Research has revealed that manual testing methods have struggled to pro-vide the comprehensive coverage and fast feedback loop which are required by modern agile and DevOps development lifecycles (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024). Moreover, researchers have found that manual testing has been time-consuming, error-prone and has often failed to scale with the growing complexity of modern web-based HMIs (Himanshu, n.d.). Although exten-sive work has advanced automated user interface (UI) testing for general web applications, no dedicated framework has been designed for industrial adoption in the high-throughput, safety-critical HMI domain (Iva, et al., 2025). Furthermore, recent evaluations have compared the of leading capa-bilities automated testing tools but have not suggested on a single, unified framework or provided definitive guidance adapted to industrial HMI envi-ronments.

Recently, several comparative studies have evaluated automated UI tools for industrial HMIs, such as Selenium and Playwright. These studies report that while Selenium's mature ecosystem provides broad browser support, its synchronization challenges make it less reliable for dynamic interfaces (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024). On the other hand, Playwright's native auto-waiting and cross-browser contexts are promising for more reliable HMI test execution, along with its easy integration into CI/CD pipelines. Further-more, recent case studies have demonstrated that these advanced frame-works can capture both technical performance metrics and usability indica-tors under realistic operational conditions, closing gaps left by manual methods (Saad, et al., 2025) (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024)

One promising solution for addressing the lack of specialized testing frame-works in industrial HMI environments would be to embed an end-to-end automated test pipeline into CI/CD workflow - architecture design bench-marked against industrial standards - so that every interface update auto-matically triggers graphical, functional, and performance checks. This solu-tion leverages the built-in synchronization and multi-browser support of modern end-to-end frameworks to minimize flakiness on dynamic indus-trial HMIs, while its continuous CI/CD integration offers the rapid feedback which is essential to agile and DevOps practices. Furthermore, by evaluat-ing the framework against industrial standards ISO 9241-210:2010 and ANSI/ISA-101.01- 2015, this evaluation ensures the technical robustness and compliance of the framework with established safety benchmarks in in-dustrial factory.

Therefore, the aim of this thesis is to design, implement and evaluate an end-to-end automated testing framework embedding Playwright tests into the CI/CD pipelines. The framework will replace the current manual test-ing, providing repeatable feedback on functional correctness and real-time performance at every HMI update regardless of the size of the change. To realise this aim, the thesis will identify the most suitable architectural ap-proach for automated testing, accomplished by conducting comparative analysis of different testing frameworks, focusing on their capabilities for CI/CD integration as well as evaluating their cost-effectiveness and long-term maintainability (Rudolf, et al., 2014). The framework in this thesis fo-cuses on simulating typical operator interaction flows to ensure the test case covers the most critical features in operating a power plant. Additionally, this thesis also studies and discusses the potential integration of interna-tional standards and best practices to ensure that the testing framework meets the strict industry benchmarks. The industrial standards ISO 9241-210:2010 and ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 are used as guidelines of critical re-quirements to inform the design and evaluation of HMIs in automation sys-tems (ISO, 2019) (Automation, 2015)

The scope of this thesis is limited to the implementation and evaluation of end-to- end automated testing framework for web-based HMIs used in power-plant control rooms. It addresses the front-end interface layer and assumes that the underlying control-system APIs and back-end services are already functionally correct. The work focuses on simulated user-flow sce-narios rather than live operator trials and on continuous integration within an existing CI/CD pipeline. Unit testing and hardware validation are not considered in this thesis. The comparative tool analysis is limited to popu-lar, open-source end-to-end frameworks and excludes record-and-playback solutions. The framework in the thesis is limited to applying best practice and discussing the potential of selectively integrating industrial standards to further enhance system reliability and performance in future iterations.

These industrial standards are used as guidelines and benchmarks for eval-uating the framework; however, the implementation of these guidelines is beyond the scope of this thesis.

The remainder of the thesis is organized as follows. Chapter 2 provides a comprehensive literature review of automated HMI testing, covering soft-ware-testing fundamentals, end-to-end (E2E) practices, and relevant inter-national standards. Chapter 3 presents the project overview, objectives and insights gained from stakeholder consultations. Chapter 4 describes the framework design, explaining evaluation criteria, tool comparison, overall architecture, CI/CD, alignment with industry standards and best practices. Chapter 5 documents the practical implementation, including server setup, test development and metrics gathered from real-world test runs. Chapter 6 discusses and analyses the framework's performance, scalability and current limitations. Chapter 7 concludes the thesis by summarizing key findings, highlighting contributions, and reflecting on the framework's impact. Fi-nally, Chapter 8 proposes directions for future work-to further enhance the robustness and usability of automated HMI testing in safety-critical environ-ments.

# Literature review

## Software testing

Software testing is a process in which to find issues of a software application, verifying that it meets all technical and non-technical requirements and en-suring fitness for its intended use (Anon., 2021). It includes verification, which checks that the product has been built correctly according to its speci-fications, and validation confirming that the finished product is the right one for its intended purpose. Therefore, software testing helps to reduce the risk of costly failures and increase the user satisfaction level (Rex, et al., 2009). Empirical study reveals that the later the defects are found in the develop-ment process, the more dramatical escalation of the cost of correcting them. Defects found in production may cost one hundred times more than found during the early stage of the development (Rex, et al., 2009).

There are multiple testing approaches that are categorized by executing method which are manual and automated - and by the testing scope, includ-ing functional and non-functional testing (Vəhid & Mika, 2016). Manual tests are performed by human testers, remains essential for evaluating user expe-rience, accessibility, and domain specific behaviours that defy automation. On the other hand, automated testing utilizes programmed test cases and specialised testing frameworks to execute repeatable tests rapidly, making it indispensable for regression validation and continuous integration pipelines (Vəhid & Mika, 2016). Functional tests confirm conformance to requirements at the unit, integration, system, and end to end levels, whereas nonfunctional tests assess performance, scalability, security, and other quality attributes (Vəhid & Mika, 2016). In this thesis, we focus on automated testing.

### Automated testing

Testing of software has been remarkably evolving over the past few years, transforming from mainly manual approaches to highly automated frame-works supporting continuous integration and agile development.

One of the earliest and most widely adopted automated testing tools is Sele-nium WebDriver. Selenium gained attraction from community due to its open-source nature, support for various programming languages as well as cross browser integrating compatibility. The ability to simulate user interac-tions and running test scripts across environments made it a foundation of automated web application testing. However, despite its strengths, Selenium faces challenges when dealing with modern web interfaces that involve

dynamic content loading and asynchronous functions, leading to unstable and fragile tests that require frequent maintenance (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024).

In recent years, Microsoft's Playwright has emerged as a modern alternative as a response to some of Selenium limitations. Playwright has functions such as native auto-waiting, minimizing the risk of flaky tests, as well as multi-browser context simulation, assuring consistent behaviours across different browsers. Moreover, Playwright designs facilitate flawless integration with CI/CD pipelines, which enables more efficient and scalable test execution in agile development (Saad, et al., 2025).

Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that although the initial invest-ment in automated test development can be substantially higher than man-ual testing, the potential for repeated execution and early defect detection results in significant cost savings over time, yielding a high ROI in the long term. Furthermore, prioritization models have been proposed to compare the manual testing effort against automation costs, thereby identifying which test cases should be automated to maximize efficiency. However, challenges such as technical debt and maintenance overhead remain significant imped-iments that must be addressed to ensure long-term reliability (Rudolf, et al., 2014)

Although automated testing has great advantages, automation requires sig-nificant initial investment and ongoing effort of maintenance. Automated test case can become brittle, being prone to false positives when application changes alter element identifiers and may impart a false sense of security if coverage is incomplete, or tests are not routinely updated. Therefore, the de-velopment team must weight automated and manual efforts according to risk, complexity, and resource constraints, embedding testing activities early and continuously throughout the development life cycle to have the highest yields return on investment (Rex, et al., 2009).

### Criteria for Automated Testing

Deciding which application, we need to automate testing is critical for cost-effective. Research (Vəhid & Mika, 2016) identify five factors that favour automation:

- - - - The life cycle of software is long - The upfront investment of automation is manageable - Development process generates a relatively big number of builds - Automated analysis of the test output is straightforward - Tests need to run against multiple hardware and software environ-ments

Selecting an appropriate automation tool and framework requires under-standing their language support, browser compatibility, learning curve, and community backing. Therefore, expertise in testing tools is fundamental to effective automation.

### End-to-end testing

Nowadays, web applications are more and more complex in architecture and modules, which are built on multiple layers and distributed across different devices (Maurizio, et al., n.d.). End-to-end (E2E) testing is designed to test the software application modules, which is one of the most popular test strat-egies in software development and performed along with unit and integration testing (Maurizio, et al., 2016)

E2E testing occupies the highest tier of the testing pyramid. It validates com-prehensive user workflows in a production-like environment. Contrasted from unit and integration testing, which validate individual components or discrete interfaces. E2E test mimic the practical user interaction flow with the software throughout the whole technology stack It includes user interface level to services, APIs, and data storage, to assure that the software behaves as expected and all the components and subsystems are correctly tightened and exercised together as a whole (Pittet, n.d.). Therefore, E2E testing is es-sential for finding the defects that emerge when modules integrate and inter-act, providing the strongest assurance of system reliability and user satisfac-tion.

A critical prerequisite for robust E2E automation is reliable element localisa-tion. DOM based localization leverages the browser's Document Object Model to identify UI elements by attributes such as id. This flexibility enables straightforward test authoring but renders the tests fragile to source-code changes. (Maurizio, et al., 2016). Alternative strategies, including coordinate based and visual pattern localisation, trade maintainability for resilience against UI refactoring but often incur higher implementation complexity and lower performance.

### Best practices for E2E testing

Strategic prioritization and meticulous execution are essential for an E2E testing program to be effective. First, the test scenarios have to be selected based on risk basis, focusing on business-critical user work flows, in which a failure could lead to catastrophic operational or financial impact (Margot & Mallory, 2020) (Anon., 2020). Test should be designed as small, self-con-tained units that are independent of one another, enabling rapid error diag-nosis and minimizing cascading failures. Cooperation among stakeholders,

including product management, user experience designers, and software en-gineers, is crucial to assure that test cases accurately reflect end user behav-iour and evolving requirements (Anon., 2020).

From technical point of view, stability and reproducibility are significant. In order to improve flakiness caused by dynamic content and asynchronous functions, automated test must use reliable locator strategies such as explicit data-testid attributes and explicit synchronization constructs (Vəhid & Mika, 2016). The test should be executed in a production-like environment to elim-inate environment variability and assure that test results are reproducible and meaningful. Finally, E2E testing framework should be integrated into CI/CD pipeline, enabling test cases to be automatically executed on every change of the codebase. That brings the benefits of fast regression detection and a rapid continuous feedback loop, which is greatly beneficial for agile delivery.

### Test case design

E2E testing is involved around the five core stages, including test scenarios design, test case scripting, execution, valuation and result reporting, which together construct a continuous feedback loop that pushes ongoing improve-ment in software development (Vəhid & Mika, 2016). This lifecycle ensures that defects introduced at any stage of development are detected as early as possible, reducing cost of correction and accelerating release speed.

A test scenario is a structural specification of predefined conditions, inputs, test cases and expected result designed to verify a slice of application func-tionality (Devaraj, 2025). Well-designed test scenarios define testing goals before any implementation, reducing ambiguity and improving maintaina-bility as well as defect finding ability. Other than striving for exhaustive cov-erage, developers should decide which scenarios are needed for test coverage, based on business impact and user criticality. That would ensure that the most critical workflows receive the highest level of assurance.

In general, test cases should be atomic, meaning they should have one simple objective that tests one function at a time. Moreover, each test should be re-peatable and self-contained, one test does not have dependency on the status of the other ones, minimizing interdependencies and simplify root cause analysis when failures occur.

One of the five core stages of test is test scripting, translating test case defi-nitions into executable code that drives the application under test via a cho-sen framework. Semantic DOM selectors, which is considered as reliable el-ement localizing solution, and clear synchronization constructs such as auto

wait are essential to minimize flakiness caused by dynamic content and asyn-chronous operations (Maurizio, et al., n.d.) (Anon., 2020).

Execution of E2E test suites is performed within the chosen automation framework, with test results are captured and logged for post analysis. Tests are often carried out in a test-dedicated environment, ideally a controlled replica of production, which enables consistent, reproducible outcomes and isolation from development or live data. Standard practice separates devel-opment, testing, and production environments to prevent unintended side effects. Testing environments should have ability to reset of test data between test runs to maintain reliability and repeatability. Evaluation of test result separate true failures from false positives. Finding and improving flaky tests is significant to maintain a certain level of confidence in the test process, along with CICD dashboards insights analytic on failure trends and stability metrics over a course of time (Jetbrains, n.d.). Finally, a comprehensive re-port, delivering test result, execution duration, and failure artifacts (screen-shots/videos) in a format user friendly format, allowing stakeholders to clas-sify issues and continuously monitor software applications health (Schmitt, 2024)

### Human-Machine Interfaces in Safety-Critical Systems

Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) is playing a significant role in operation of safety-critical industrial systems, serving as the most important link through which operators interact with complex control systems. In industrial systems, HMIs are responsible for transforming raw sensor data into action-able information, thereby enabling real-time decision-making that is crucial for maintaining operational safety (Chuanzan, et al., 2020).

The design of HMIs in power plant is remarkably challenging due to the need to balance technical functionality with ergonomic and usability require-ments. Research has shown that poor interface design can significantly con-tribute to operator failure, with evident historical incidents such as a series of mistakes leading to the Chernobyl disaster, revealing the consequences of inadequate system feedback and poor design (Chuanzan, et al., 2020). There-fore, a robust HMI design must emphasize clarity, consistency, and intuitive operation to reduce the risks and improve system performance.

International standards lay a solid foundation for resolving these challenges. One of those standards, ISO 9241-210 frameworks human-centered design principles encouraging user-friendly and ergonomically sound interfaces, which assures that HMIs designs meet the cognitive and physical capabilities of their operators (ISO, 2019). ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 lays out the critical re-quirements in designing HMIs, especially emphasizing safety, clarity, and

effective operator interaction (Automation, 2015). Although these standards offer comprehensive guidelines, their full implementation in any project can be challenging. However, they serve as a benchmark for evaluating and im-proving HMI designs in safety-critical environments (Eduard, et al., 2017) Recent research continues to study innovative approaches to improve HMI performance, focusing more on integrating advanced technologies and auto-mation to reduce human error. These studies, emphasize the importance of systematic test and continuous evaluation HMI to assure that they not merely meet all the technical requirements but also effectively support operator per-formance in real-work conditions (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024) (Chuanzan, et al., 2020).

## Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment in Automated Testing

Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) have become foundational practices in software development, particularly in agile and DevOps environments in the recent years. The integration of automated test-ing frameworks with CI/CD pipelines allows the immediate performance of test cases on every code commit event, reducing the time between code changes and the detection of issues (Jetbrains, n.d.). The continuous loop of feedback is crucial for maintaining the stability of complex systems such as web-based HMIs, where any delay in detecting issues can have significant operational downtime.

CI/CD pipelines facilitate not merely the automation of test performing but also the standardized test report management, providing insight into key performance measures such as the ratio of pass/fail tests, failure occurrences and execution duration. This reporting architecture is significant in monitor-ing software quality over a course of time and supports the iterative improve-ment of both the testing process and the overall system. Moreover, contain-erized testing environments, enabled by technologies, for instance, Docker, help ensure consistency across different stages of deployment, further en-hancing the reliability of the testing process (Jetbrains, n.d.).

Modern testing tools, such as Microsoft's Playwright, are designed with CI/CD integration as one of a must-have prerequisite. Playwright's native support for automated workflows allows for a smooth incorporation into CI/CD systems such as Bamboo, GitHub Actions, or Bitbucket pipelines. It is crucial for reaching the stage of fast regression detection and effective maintenance in rapid pace of modern software development. Effective CI/CD integration not merely accelerates up feedback loops but also being signifi-cant contributing factor in improving test coverage and reliability of the whole system (Beata & Agnieszka, 2024) (Jetbrains, n.d.)

## Data Generation and Reporting in Automated Testing

Automated testing frameworks not only perform tests repeatedly but also en-able generating report of performance data, which is important component for assessing system reliability and the effectiveness of the test. Recording the most important technical metrics like uptime, error rates, is important to maintain continuous, quantitative feedback. These technical measures pro-vide developers insight into health of the system over a course of time and identify trends that may indicate emerging issues before they escalate into serious problems (Chuanzan, et al., 2020) (Dorothy, et al., n.d.)

In practice, automated test reports should be structured to provide a clear, and actionable information of the software's behaviours under testing. Best practices in test reporting suggest that metrics should be presented in stand-ardized formats in order to facilitate integration with CI/CD pipelines and to be readable by both technical Comparative Analysis of Manual vs. Automated Testing Effort and Effectiveness and non-technical stakeholders. These re-ports generally include summary statistics for each test execution, along with detailed logs that document individual test results, execution times, and any encountered errors (Jetbrains, n.d.). This level of reporting ensures that each test run can be analysed independently, enabling teams to quickly isolate and address any issues without the need for aggregating data from multiple test cycles. Effective reporting design are essential for continuous improvement. Reports should be designed to trigger alerts when important thresholds are crossed, for instance, if error rates exceed acceptable limits or if response times degrade over consecutive test cycles. By integrating these best practices into test report design, teams can ensure that the automated testing frame-work not only detects defects promptly but also provides insights that guide iterative enhancements in both the software and the test process (Eduard, et al., 2017)

## Comparative Analysis of Manual vs. Automated Testing Effort and Effectiveness

Research consistently reveals that automated test, while requiring a higher initial investment in terms of time and resources, can gain significant long-term benefits compared to manual testing. Early research in software testing highlights that manual testing, despite its strengths in exploring ad hoc sce-narios and assessing user experience, is labour-intensive and prone to hu-man mistake (Rex, et al., 2009). As software systems have grown in complex-ity, the limitations of manual testing, such as inability to scale and its incon-sistent repeatability, have become increasingly apparent.

Several case studies, particularly in industrial control environments, have compared the cost, effort, and defect detection capabilities of manual versus automated testing. These studies indicate that automated tests, once devel-oped, can be executed repeatedly with minimal additional cost, thereby sig-nificantly reducing the overall testing effort over time. For example, studies of industrial control software have found that automated test suites can de-liver the same level of code coverage as manual testing, yet they operate in a fraction of the time, leading to earlier defect detection and lower long-term costs (Eduard, et al., 2017). Such findings underscore the importance of pri-oritizing test cases for automation, ensuring that tests with the highest po-tential for repeated execution and defect detection are selected first.

In addition, models for prioritization have been proposed that evaluate test cases based on the manual effort required versus the anticipated benefits of automation. These models help organizations identify which tests should be automated to maximize ROI. By quantifying factors such as the cost of man-ual execution, the frequency of test runs, and the potential impact of unde-tected defects, these models provide a structured approach to test selection and scheduling. Although the cost of developing automated tests is generally higher, the cumulative savings in execution time and improved defect detec-tion make automation a strategic investment, particularly in safety-critical environments where the cost of failure is exceptionally high.

# Case Study

This project delivers an automated testing framework for a web-based HMI interface, which is a critical control and monitoring tool used across power plants. The interface uses the Atvise Builder, which exports production-ready JavaScript files that run in Chromium. Because those exports lack a source-code structure and are not suitable for unit and integration testing, teams have relied on manual validation. This testing approach is not only la-bour-intensive and error-prone but also repeatedly consumes valuable re-sources every time a change is made.

The HMI must support a variety of plant configurations by adapting its layout and behavior in two ways: by re-exporting updated files from Atvise or by invoking internal browser APIs at runtime. Effective testing therefore re-quires not only verifying that the graphical interface renders correctly but also confirming that each configuration change produces the intended func-tionality. Manual testing for various versions of HMI is unsustainable.

To address this, we embed our E2E suite into Bitbucket via a Bamboo plan that spins up Docker containers on each commit. Those containers run Playwright against the deployed HMI and block any merge if tests fail. This automation reduces human error prone with faster feedback as well as frees engineering resources for more important engineer tasks.

## Motivation

The motivation of this project is from the limitations of our current testing methods. Manual testing of Atvise-exported JavaScript reveals two major challenges. The first challenge is that the building artifacts are monolith ar-chitecture and lack modularity codebase, making unit tests impractical. Other issue is that the HMI's dynamic configuration options multiply the number of manual test scenarios required. In a safety-critical environment, these gaps endanger product integrity and amplify the risk of undetected de-fects. Automated E2E testing framework can ensure that every change, from simple UI modification to bigger update, is reliably verified before deploy-ment.

## System Context

The HMI operates within a complex, configurable ecosystem. Atvise exports form the core interface, but runtime behaviours can also be altered via pro-prietary browser APIs. This dual-configuration mechanism supports scenar-ios ranging from small turbine controls to full-scale grid management.

Consequently, our framework must verify that the user interface renders and responds correctly under every configuration, confirm that configura-tion API calls drive the intended system behaviours, and integrate smoothly with existing build infrastructure (Bitbucket, Bamboo, Docker). Automated, end-to-end testing is therefore essential to guarantee production quality across all supported plant configurations.

## Objectives and limitations

The primary goal of the project is to validate both the visualization of the in-terface and the configuration logic of the HMI on each commit. The solution must validate that screens, transitions, and user interactions work as de-signed, that critical internal API calls make the expected HMI transition. These tests play an important role in determining whether a commit should be merged based on whether the critical features pass predefined quality cri-teria.

However, we also faced several limitations. The JavaScript exported by At-vise is complex, bundled code that is not structured for unit testing, forcing reliance on end-to-end tests even more. The HMI server's licensing mecha-nism adds an operational overhead that must be automated so that we can run multiple containers for parallel tests. The complexity of configuration logic requires a set of flexible test cases which are capable of handling vari-ous workflows and edge cases. Moreover, the requirement is also that the solution must run within our existing Bamboo infrastructure and additional platforms or tools should be avoided if possible.

To handle those challenges, the project involves extensive discussions and interviews with the HMI engineers as well as system engineers. These con-sultations help refine the testing requirements by identifying which user sce-narios and critical API functions are "must-have". With their help, we also define qualitative criteria such as execution duration, test coverage as bench-marks for the framework. The understanding of both the operational envi-ronment and the technical limitations helps laying the solid foundation the framework architecture design.

## Stakeholder consultations

The design of our testing framework was grounded in a series of in-depth consultations with key stakeholders, starting primarily with HMI developers and system engineers, whose insights ensured that our solution addressed practical challenges. In the first workshop, we discussed the existing manual testing process, mapping each step from code export through deployment

and identifying the most time-consuming and error-prone workflows. More-over, system engineers demonstrated their daily work related to HMI config-uring and how complex configuration combinations and ad-hoc API calls cur-rently demanded extensive human verification. These discussions empha-sized the critical need of an automated test framework.

Extending from the understandings of the first meeting, the second session focused to defining the precise testing scenarios that must be covered. We walked through user journeys, such as how user navigate between screens, trigger alarm dialogs, and apply configuration profiles via internal APIs, to capture both UI and API interactions. This collaborative modelling of test scenarios validated that the Page Object Model would accommodate the HMI's dual configuration paths and highlighted the necessity of end-to-end scripts that could both manipulate runtime settings and verify visual changes. This discussion lay the foundation for the E2E framework require-ment, which is used as the benchmark to select the correct tools.

In the final discussion, we presented our proposed CI/CD integrated archi-tecture and solicited feedback on integration points with Bitbucket, Bamboo, and our Ubuntu server environment. Stakeholders with the proposal that embedding test execution directly into the pull-request workflow (PR) would deliver the fastest feedback loop as well as align with existing operational practices. Engineers also emphasized the importance of clear reporting, link-ing build artifacts back to specific commits and configuration versions. It al-lows developers and operators trace any failure back to its root cause.

These three iterative workshops not only refined the technical requirements, defining which UI elements and API calls are non-negotiable test targets, but also shaped development team experience goals for test reporting and feed-back. By engaging stakeholders at every stage, we have ensured that the framework is both technically appropriate and a solution for the practical challenges we have.

With requirements and constraints firmly established through stakeholder workshops, Chapter 4 describes our architecture and the technical realiza-tion of this testing framework.

# Framework Design

In safety-critical power-plant environments, every HMI change must be val-idated in a production like setting before released. This chapter describes the design of our automated E2E testing framework, which integrates Bit-bucket, Bamboo, Docker, and Playwright, to guarantee fast, reliable feed-back on every commit and prevent regressions in Human-Machine Inter-faces.

## Overall Framework Architecture

The proposed solution automatically validates web-based Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) by embedding e2e tests into a Bamboo integrated CI/CD pipeline. Each change commit in HMI repository in Bitbucket triggers a test plan, ensuring consistency and reproducibility by encapsulating all depend-encies and environment configurations.

The automated testing layer is built around the Playwright framework, which we drive through a TypeScript interface to design, execute and maintain our E2E test cases. By leveraging Playwright's built-in cross-browser support, we validate our HMI with our customized browser within our existing Sele-nium-based executable. This layer is also where test reporting is managed, deciding what data to capture, its format and stored place.

Supplement for the automated testing layer is the continuous integration, where we use Bamboo to orchestrate our test plan. Whenever a developer pushes or merges code in Bitbucket, Bamboo picks up the new commit, checks out the exact hash and spins up a fresh test environment. Playwright then runs the full suite, producing an interactive HTML report with step-by-step details alongside JUnit and JSON artifacts, plus concise console logs. Bamboo archives all these artifacts and automatically links them to the corresponding pull request, effectively blocking any merge if a test fails.

Once test cases run complete, Bamboo immediately pushes real-time notifi-cations to the development team, complete with direct links to the detailed HTML reports. This fast feedback loop keeps everyone aware of regressions and speeds up our troubleshooting cycle.

We ensure scalability by using containerization technology, in which tests ex-ecute concurrently on multiple Docker agents, and our CI/CD pipeline auto-matically adjusts resource allocation to match the workload. By defining our environments in Docker, we guarantee that our testing environment reflects environment in production closely as possible.

Design decisions support our research goals by leveraging Playwright's ro-bust handling of dynamic content and continuous integration, aligning with industry best practices for a reliable HMI testing. This integrated architec-ture delivers continuous, production-grade feedback and directly addresses the optimal architecture questions at the heart of this thesis.

## Tool Selection and Comparative Analysis

During our stakeholder engagement meeting, we establish a set of evalua-tion criteria that serve as the basis for comparing test automation frame-works. We categorize these criteria into two groups: primary requirements, which outline the essential, mission-critical functions our solution must provide, and secondary requirements, which cover supplementary features that improve usability and facilitate future extension.

### Tool selection criteria

We derived our primary requirements (refer to table 1) from hands-on ob-servations and stakeholder consultations, ensuring the framework can exe-cute custom JavaScript in the browser context while remaining compatible with Chromium-based browsers. It must accurately simulate click actions, implement wait strategies for UI elements and their dynamic properties, verify both static and localized text, and integrate smoothly with CI/CD pipelines to enforce automated gating of code changes. (Rex, et al., 2009) (Chuanzan, et al., 2020).

When comparing the frameworks, its evident that while all of them meet the base-line requirements, differences are in their advanced features and overall usability. Selenium is recognized for its mature ecosystem and excellent multi-language sup-port, which makes it appealing for the team to need a versatile solution. However, its approach to handling dynamic content often requires additional effort with

explicit waiting conditions and more complex locator strategies. This can make maintenance more cumbersome in our highly dynamic HMI testing environments.

Cypress, with its intuitive API and strong native support for JavaScript, is great in simulating user interactions and offers automatic waiting mechanisms that sim-plify the test development process. Its reporting and integration with CI/CD pipe-lines are robust, making it attractive for iterative testing environments. However, its native focus on JavaScript, without strong Python support, is limitation.

Nightwatch, which builds upon Selenium, provides reliable automation and user interaction simulation but unfortunately inherits some of Selenium's limitations when it comes to handling dynamic UI changes. Its design is straightforward if team already invested in the Selenium ecosystem, yet it does not introduce the modern improvements seen in more recent frameworks.

Playwright distinguishes itself by combining the best attributes from the other frameworks. It natively supports custom JavaScript execution in a streamlined way and provides a sophisticated, built-in auto-waiting mechanism that minimizes test flakiness which is a crucial component in dynamic HMI testing. Furthermore, Playwright's strong support for Python enhances its flexibility while maintaining robust native capabilities in JavaScript. Its friendly integration with CI/CD sys-tems through multiple reporting formats is a good contributing factor to a fast con-tinuous feedback loop.

## Framework architecture

Building on the project goal laid out in section 3.3, the framework testing layers is integrated with our CICD pipeline. The source code of HMI is man-aged in Bitbucket, where each code commit immediately triggers a Bamboo test plan. This plan orchestrates the entire testing process, starting from es-tablishing a secure SSH connection to a dedicated Ubuntu test server.

By encapsulating all necessary dependencies, including Node.js, Playwright, browser engines, and custom libraries, within a pre-built Docker image, the framework minimizes the setup time and eliminates residual state between test executions, ensure consistency over test runs. Docker launches the con-tainer (see 4.4.3), in which Playwright runs our end-to-end suite against the deployed HMI application.

These tests are designed to simulate practical user workflows and critical component interactions of the HMI. They cover scenarios such as screen transitions, error handling, user interaction patterns, and complex HMI con-figuration process via internal API response validations. The test cases are developed in a modular fashion, following best practices Page Object Model for better maintenance as well as scalability.

As the tests run, detailed logs, screenshots, and trace captures are generated. The results are compiled into structured reports in multiple formats (see 4.4.4) and are stored as build artifacts within Bamboo. Each test run is assigned a unique URL, providing immediate access to the comprehensive test results.

Finally, the framework integrates tightly with Bitbucket. Based on the test outcomes, Bamboo communicates back to Bitbucket by posting a message on pull requests with a direct link to the test manifest. If tests fail, the corre-sponding pull request would be blocked from merging until the issues are resolved. This immediate feedback loop ensures that only code meeting our quality standards is integrated into production, thereby minimizing potential risks of bugs in production.

Figure 1. CI/CD-integrated E2E testing pipeline for the HMI application

### Playwright

Our Playwright configuration is designed to support test execution environ-ment within our automated testing framework with the scalability in mind. This section outlines all key technical details and choices that ensure our E2E tests are executed reliably in a containerized environment and well in-tegrated with our CI/CD pipeline.

First, Playwright is configured to run in headless mode, which is essential for resource conservation and optimal performance within the pre-built Docker image. The configuration below lives in playwright.config.js (refer to Appendix A)

Running in headless mode significantly speeds up test execution while still providing consistent behavior across different runs. The configuration de-fines a fixed viewport of 1280 x 720 pixels, which matches the exact resolu-tion of our HMI display, to ensure that the tests accurately simulate the user interface used in production. Furthermore, the configuration specifies

the use of the Chromium browser, particularly via the Chrome channel. This choice supports our requirement for stability and compatibility, given that our HMI application is heavily optimized for Chromium-based environ-ments. We ignore HTTPS errors so that self-signed certificates do not halt critical tests.

Detailed logging is an important aspect of our test strategy. Our setup uses Playwright's test.step() to highlight key actions in each test case. This cre-ates clear narrative in the HTML report, making it easier to troubleshoot when failures occur. The configuration also enables the trace: 'retain-on-failure' option. In the event of a test failure, this feature captures compre-hensive trace data, including browser state snapshots, DOM structure at failure points, network log details, and console outputs. Although the setup currently captures discrete data points, it lays the groundwork for potential future enhancements such as selective video capture and historical data.

Our configuration specifies three primary reporters:

- An interactive HTML reporter that creates detailed, navigable re-ports with integrated screenshots and trace logs.
- A JUnit reporter that outputs XML-formatted data for friendly inte-gration with our CI system, Bamboo, which relies on these reports for automated build status updates.
- A JSON reporter that produces structured data for further analysis and trend monitoring.

Besides, flexibility is built into our configuration through the use of environ-ment variables. Inside Docker container, the

PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH environment variable is set, allowing us to specify a custom browser executable path. This is especially useful for accommodating updates or using particular browser builds without altering the core configuration file. Moreover, the configuration includes dynamic settings via Node.js, including reading a list of test cases from an environ-ment variable (TEST_CASE) so that specific test suites can be targeted dur-ing different runs.

The main configuration is defined in the playwright.config.js file, including all the setup details discussed above. It also specifies the test directory, max-imum number of worker processes, and retry logic to ensure parallel test ex-ecution capability and balance resource use at the same time. The configura-tion is supported by a corresponding TypeScript configuration (tscon-fig.json), which enforces strict type-checking and ensures that our test code follow to modern JavaScript standards (ES2021).

### Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment

Our CI/CD integration process is the backbone of our automated testing framework orchestration, ensuring that every change to the HMI application is immediately validated before merging. When a developer commits code to Bitbucket, a webhook immediately triggers a preconfigured Bamboo build plan. This build plan orchestrates the entire workflow, from establishing se-cure connections to remotely provisioning environments, all the way through test execution, artifact collection, and feedback integration.

The process begins when a code commits triggers Bamboo. In our Bamboo YAML configuration, the plan first checks out the repository and sets up nec-essary build variables.

The next steps in the sequence, Bamboo establishes a secure SSH connection to a dedicated Ubuntu test server. This is accomplished by decoding an AWS SSH key and adding the host to the known_hosts file to ensure secure con-nectivity. Below is an excerpt that shows this SSH preparation (refer to Ap-pendix B)

Once the SSH tunnel is in place, the environment is set up using Docker. A pre-built Docker image, configured with all necessary dependencies (Node.js, Playwright, browser engines, and additional utilities), is launched on the re-mote server.

This containerized approach guarantees a consistent environment for each test run. It also reduces setup overhead. Once the container is up, it

automatically pulls the latest version of the HMI application and begins ex-ecuting our test case of E2E tests with Playwright.

As the tests execute inside the Docker container, detailed logs, screenshots, and trace data are generated. These artifacts are stored in the designated playwright-report directory, which is mounted as part of the build environ-ment so that Bamboo can collect them automatically. Once the test run is completed, the Docker container is dropped immediately, ensuring no resid-ual state remains.

![Ảnh có chứa văn bản, biểu đồ, ảnh chụp màn hình, Song song  Nội dung do AI tạo ra có thể không chính xác.](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Playwright CI/CD Test Execution and Reporting Pipeline

Upon completion of the tests, Bamboo collects the test artifacts (HTML, JSON, and JUnit reports) into a build manifest. A unique URL is generated for each test run, making the detailed test report accessible immediately. This URL is then integrated back into Bitbucket's pull request workflow. Because the build was originally triggered by a Bitbucket push or pull-request event, Bamboo automatically exposes the corresponding commit SHA and pull-re-quest ID in environment variables (bamboo.repository.revision and bam-boo.bitbucket.pr.id). These variables serve as the definitive link between the test results and the exact code change under review (refer to Appendix C).

Besides the Bitbucket update, the same script sends a JSON payload to the team's Slack incoming-webhook URL (<https://hooks.slack.com/ser-vices/>&lt;...&gt;). This payload includes the plan key, build number, commit SHA, pull-request link, and manifest URL. In Slack, the notification appears in the designated channel as

\[&lt;PLAN_KEY&gt;-&lt;BUILD_NUMBER&gt;\] E2E tests for PR #&lt;PR_ID&gt; (commit &lt;COMMIT_SHA&gt;) have &lt;sta-tus&gt;. View full results → &lt;manifest URL&gt;

This tight feedback loop ensures that if any test fails, the PR merge is auto-matically blocked, and developers and stakeholders receive immediate noti-fication along with a direct link to the test results. In contrast, a passing test run allows PR to proceed. This integration not only enhances development agility but also maintains a high standard of quality control, essential for a safety-critical system such as a power plant HMI.

### Docker image

Our test container is built upon Microsoft's official Playwright image (mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:next), which already includes Playwright, Node.js. We layer on essential utilities, including Git, tmux, build-essential, and Bash, and immediately cleaning up package metadata with rm -rf

/var/lib/apt/lists/\* to minimize image size and maximize caching efficiency. The Dockerfile sets the working directory to /project, ensures the Playwright binaries are executable, and switches to the root user to allow system instal-lations and repository cloning (refer to Appendix C).

The core of our container orchestration is the entrypoint.sh script, beginning by echoing its start time and environment variables for easier troubleshoot-ing. It then removes any existing checkout of the HMI code, clones the repos-itory over SSH, and checks out the designated feature branch (refer to Ap-pendix D).

Within the test/test-scripts directory, dependencies for test framework are installed via Yarn, customized Chromium executable is fetched. It use the PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH environment variable value as the path to find the browser executables. Besides, permissions must be grant to ensure Playwright has access to the browser binaries.

Once the code and dependencies are in place, the script returns to the project root to run the Webpack build, which is then used to spin up the HMI. The database file (nodes.db) and external assets (web and dist) are the core of HMI, which is output of Webpack build process, copied into a Atvise dedi-cated server directory. Finally, Playwright's end-to-end tests are executed in headless mode with tracing enabled, and any failures result in a non-zero exit code that Bamboo will detect and report.

In our Docker Compose setup, we mount the host's SSH keys into the con-tainer to permit Git authentication and bind the playwright-report directory back to the Bamboo workspace so that HTML reports, JUnit XML, and JSON results are automatically collected as build artifacts. Port 80 is exposed on the Docker host to allow the Atvise server running inside the container to handle API validations against a live HMI backend instance running on the host, Ubuntu server. All critical values like repository URL, branch name, browser binaries path, and report directories, are all injected via environ-ment variables, providing full flexibility to switch branches, toggle additional diagnostics, or point to alternative browser builds without modifying the Docker image itself.

### Report

Our reporting setup provides detailed visibility into each test run, offering both summaries and diagnostic information for thorough review. The main output is HTML report, which offers visual detailed overview of the test exe-cution. This report summarizes the total number of tests executed along with the counts of passed, failed, and skipped tests, while also providing a step-by-step breakdown of each test scenario. Moreover, the report also include execution timings and step statuses, with embedded screenshots and trace captures for any failures when the 'retain-on-failure' setting is activated. Us-ers can interactively navigate through this report, checking individual test cases to review the sequence of operations, which is particularly useful for finding issues and understanding system behaviours under various test cases.

In addition to the HTML report, our system generates a standardized JUnit XML report. This report is structured according to the JUnit schema, ensur-ing that it well integrates with our CI/CD. The JUnit output has key perfor-mance metrics at the test suite level, including the execution time for each test case, overall test counts, and detailed descriptions of any failures, stack traces and error messages. It enables automated build status reporting and facilitating rapid issue identification within CICD debugger. Moreover, this structured data serves as the backbone for aggregating test results across multiple runs, laying foundation for future improvement in which we collect and analyse metrics across multiple tests.

The last one is JSON report, offering detailed collection of metadata that cap-tures the states of individual test cases. The JSON is highly compatible for-mat, as it can be parsed by various external tools to extract custom metrics, visualize trends via dashboards, or even feed into advanced analytical sys-tems. The raw, detailed data available in this format provides a foundation for performing retrospective analyses and continuous performance optimi-zations, ensuring that we can correlate test outcomes with changes in the ap-plication over time and over test cases.

During test execution, our framework simultaneously leverages a line re-porter that outputs real-time, concise logs directly to the Bamboo CI/CD con-sole. This live stream of updates is optimized to provide immediate feedback on the progression of the test suite, indicating when individual tests start, finish, or fail without overwhelming the user with excessive detail. The min-imal overhead provided by the line reporter ensures that the critical infor-mation is available immediately, allowing developers and testers to quickly action overall system health as tests run.

## Application of International Standards

The quality and usability of Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) in safety-critical environments are regulated by international standards designed to ensure that interfaces are both efficient and user-friendly.

In our framework design, although full compliance with these standards is not currently implemented, we have intentionally used them as benchmarks to guide our evaluation and set a foundation for future enhancement.

The first standard we researched in this study, ISO 9241 210, emphasizing a human-centred design approach that prioritizes usability and the minimiza-tion of user errors. It offers essential guidance on crafting interfaces that align with operator cognitive and physical abilities (ISO, 2019). Similarly, ANSI/ISA 101.01 2015 outlines detailed requirements for HMIs used in

process automation systems, focusing on clear communication, consistency, and safety, which are essential for preventing costly errors in high-risk oper-ational settings (Automation, 2015).

In this section, we mainly assess how our current framework aligns with these international guidelines and identify specific areas where further inte-gration could enhance both test design and overall system evaluation. By mapping our framework's features against the key elements of these stand-ards, we reveal that while our approach already meets many operational re-quirements, there are always opportunities to incorporate additional ergo-nomic and usability guidelines.

Although our primary objective in this project is to deliver a practical and efficient automated testing solution, establishing these standards as bench-marks validates our design choices and provides a clear roadmap for future enhancements. Importantly, this research lays the groundwork for a more complete integration of internationally recognized best practices into our testing framework, thereby ensuring that it can evolve to meet the highest safety and usability criteria in future iterations.

### Standard ISO

ISO 9241 210 is standard outlining specifications and guidance for applying human-centred design at every stage of interactive system development (ISO, 2019). Contrast from many other standards broadly discussing usabil-ity, ISO 9241 210 is focused on ensuring that systems are designed from a human centred perspective. It requires that design must be grounded in a deep understanding of the users, their interactions, as well as the environ-ments in which the system will be used. This requirement is crucial in safety critical settings where even small usability shortcomings can have dramatic consequences.

The standard begins by clearly defining the scope and terminology necessary for human centred design. It specifies key terms "usability," "user," and "con-text of use" in precise language so that all stakeholders have a common un-derstanding (ISO, 2019). The standard sets the stage for an iterative design process where every decision is informed by knowledge about the users and the situational context. This foundational premise is particularly valuable in our domain, where HMIs must reliably convey critical information to opera-tors under varying conditions.

The central of ISO 9241 210 are the human centred design principles. The standard states that the design is based on an explicit understanding of users, tasks, and environments. This is achieved by gathering user requirements,

analysing the context of use, and ensuring that the design process is iterative. The standard further highlights that users must be actively involved through-out the design and development process. This involvement is not limited to simple usability tests but extends to continuous user centred evaluation, whereby iterative feedback from representative users refines the design until the solution meets both functional and ergonomic requirements. Such itera-tive evaluation and refinement are emphasized as fundamental to minimiz-ing user error and improving overall system performance (ISO, 2019).

Besides that, another aspect of ISO 9241 210 is its insistence on addressing the whole user experience. The standard goes beyond mere functional cor-rectness by considering how the system affects the user in terms of comfort, satisfaction, and emotional response. It requires that designers not only as-sess whether a system achieves its intended tasks effectively but also whether the system is acceptable from a subjective, human experience perspective. This comprehensive view of usability, incorporating factors such as cognitive load, physical comfort, and even long-term satisfaction, provides a rich framework, in which our test strategies can be contextualized. In our appli-cation, incorporating principles from ISO 9241 210 would imply designing test cases that not only measure technical metrics (execution times and error rates) but also evaluate system behaviours that influence user trust and safety.

The standard also describes the process-oriented nature of human centred design. It recommends that the design process should be iterative, where pre-liminary designs are refined through continuous testing, evaluation, and in-corporation of user feedback. The iterative process described in ISO 9241 210 includes multiple cycles of prototype evaluation and redesign, ensuring that the final solution is well adapted to its intended context. For a testing frame-work, especially one aimed at HMIs in safety critical environments, this iter-ative methodology underscores the importance of continuously updating and refining automated tests to capture evolving user requirements and environ-mental constraints.

Additionally, ISO 9241 210 provides guidance on planning and managing hu-man centred design activities. It outlines how to structure design processes, develop user requirements, and establish milestones for evaluation, which are all elements that can inform the strategic planning of our future test framework enhancements. Although our current implementation does not fully integrate all these principles, the selective adoption of insights from ISO 9241 210 enables our framework to be evaluated against robust benchmarks. In doing so, we set the stage for future work where deeper integration of these principles can lead to improved usability assessments and overall system re-liability.

### ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015

ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 is a detailed standard focused on HMIs for systems in process automation. The standard provides precise requirements and guide-lines that address the entire lifecycle of HMIs, from design and implementa-tion through operation and continuous improvement. Unlike other broader usability standards, ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 concentrates on how HMIs must be designed for environments where real-time monitoring and control are critical, ensuring that operators can interact safely and effectively with com-plex automated processes (Automation, 2015).

This standard begins by clearly defining its scope and intended audience. It targets HMI designers emphasizing that the guidance applies to any auto-mated process control system, whether continuous, batch, or discrete. The standard reinforces that it is to be used as an aid in achieving improved reli-ability and quality as well as productivity in process control systems. In this way, the standard serves not only as a technical guide but also as a philosoph-ical framework for developing robust HMIs in demanding industrial con-texts.

One of the key attributes of ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 is its focus on ensuring consistency and clarity across HMI designs. The standard regulates that HMIs must provide clear visual feedback and effective error indications. It requires that displays are designed with appropriate visual cues to enable op-erators to quickly discern the status of a process and to react promptly to abnormal conditions such as color, layout, and graphic symbolism. This em-phasis on clarity is critical in environments where every second counts, and even minor misinterpretations can lead to significant operational hazards.

ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015 also outlines specific requirements related to the HMI's visual layout and interaction methods. Standard emphasizes that dis-plays should be designed not only to convey information but also to support decision-making. The arrangement of screens, the use of pop-up displays for critical alerts, and the design of navigation controls are all regulated by pre-cise guidelines aimed at reducing cognitive load and operator error. The standard requires that HMIs are developed in a way that permits rapid re-trieval of information and that they incorporate redundancy and error-toler-ant designs where necessary.

In our current testing framework, while we have not yet implemented all the aspects described by ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015, its detailed specifications pro-vide valuable benchmarks. Our automated tests currently focus on verifying

functionality and responsiveness. However, this standard reminds us that fu-ture iterations should also include assessments of visual feedback, display consistency, and user interaction patterns. Practically, the improvement in-volves developing test cases that specifically validate the clarity of error mes-sages, the consistency of layout elements across different screens, and the effectiveness of visual indicators under various simulated conditions.

### Best practice in E2E testing

E2E testing account for system workflow to reflect real user behaviours and ensure high software quality. Identifying testing strategy and critical user workflows that impact business operations is an important step. Instead of aiming for fully coverage, which can result in unwieldy test cases, teams should focus on key paths where failures would cause significant disruption. Engaging cross-functional teams, with different stakeholders, helps ensure that the strategy aligns with both user needs and technical view. Prior to test scripting, clear objectives of the test can be achieved by outlining clear test scenario, listing detailed preconditions, step sequences, and expected out-comes (Margot & Mallory, 2020).

Once these essential workflows are identified, a modular test design is the next significant step. Implementing design patterns such as the Page Object Model (POM) compress complex interactions by isolating UI elements and behaviours into dedicated objects, which simplifies maintenance as the user interface evolves and enhances the readability and reusability of the test code (Dorothy, et al., n.d.). Group test cases by functionality, application modules, or user journey stages. This organization simplifies the management of an expanding test case and aids in identifying common patterns or shared de-pendencies. It also facilitates reusability, since tests addressing similar func-tionalities can often leverage identical preconditions and helper methods. Creating reusable helper functions for common tasks reduces code duplica-tion and adjusts across multiple tests more efficient. Clear documentation through structured templates or tracking systems (Jira tickets) ensures that every test case is traceable from design through implementation. Each test case should include a brief description, list relevant preconditions, outline step-by-step actions, and specify the expected outcomes. This structured doc-umentation not only streamlines the development phase but also aids in fu-ture maintenance and troubleshooting

In parallel, modern practices emphasize the technical environment and pro-cess elements crucial to reliable testing. Containerized testing environments, such as running tests within Docker containers on dedicated servers, guar-antee that the test environment remains reproducible and isolated. It

significantly reduces setup time and minimizing environmental drift. This controlled isolation has been validated by multiple studies as a key contribu-tor to consistency across test runs (Rex, et al., 2009). Furthermore, integrat-ing the testing pipeline with version control systems and continuous deploy-ment processes creates a robust feedback loop, where continuous integration (CI) is leveraged to trigger automated test execution on every commit through CI/CD pipelines, can enable rapid feedback and early detection of defects, which ultimately reduces the overall development cycle and associ-ated costs (Chuanzan, et al., 2020).

Robust reporting is another essential aspect. The detailed and interactive HTML reports that include screenshots, trace information, and comprehen-sive logs allow developers to quickly point out the root causes of failures. Structured reports, formatted as JUnit or JSON, can friendly integrate with CI systems, supporting automated build status reporting and facilitating data-driven decision-making. Besides that, synchronization mechanisms, such as native auto-waiting and explicit wait constructs, ensure that tests only proceed once all necessary UI components have fully loaded, thereby minimizing flaky tests which is the pain point of E2E tests.

Beyond technical aspects, long-term success in E2E testing requires adaption to best practices that enhance maintainability and scalability. Tests should be organized into logical sets by functionality or user journey stages, and sta-ble selector strategies should be implemented using attributes like unique "data-testid" markers or element roles that remain consistent even if the un-derlying HTML changes. Employing fixtures to manage setup and teardown processes guarantees that tests run in isolation by always beginning from a known, controlled state (Playwright, n.d.). Additionally, a comprehensive test strategy, designed with input from cross-functional teams such as prod-uct managers, QA experts, and developers, is important to ensure that testing aligns with both user needs and technical feasibility (Golubeva, 2024).
