Our E2E suite is built to simulate practical operator workflows and environmental conditions in the HMI, ensuring that each scenario mirrors real-world usage and validates critical functionality. We begin by automating the core power-plant

operator tasks, from navigating screens, responding to the alarms system, and ap-plying configuration profiles via internal APIs, and extending coverage to the com-plex configuration variants used across different plant types. These "horizontal" test cases were defined in close collaboration with HMI engineers and system op-erators to surface the highest-priority user journeys and business requirements early in development.

Rather than simple pass/fail markers, our tests include rich assertions that verify text and layout consistency, confirm event-driven behaviors, and exercise

data-driven workflows end to end. To eliminate the flakiness that is pain point of many UI E2E test, we rely on Playwright's built-in auto-waiting and supplement it with targeted explicit waits, guaranteeing that every dynamic component is fully loaded before interaction.

We structure our tests in a modular Page Object Model, with each test functioning as an independent unit and helper functions abstracting common interactions.

This design lets us add new scenarios without touching existing code, keeping the codebase clean and easy to maintain as the HMI's complexity grows.

Our test results are constructed to generate interactive HTML reports (with screenshots, steps, and trace captures) along with structured JUnit and JSON re-ports that friendly integrate with our CI/CD system. These test reports provide im-mediate material for developers to identify the issue caused by the new change in HMI code. This instantaneous is also emphasized by our CICD pipeline design, where the reports are propagated to developers through multiple channels.

When a test run completes, Playwright generates an interactive HTML report, complete with embedded steps, screenshots, and trace captures, as well as struc-tured JUnit XML and JSON artifacts that friendly integrate with our CI/CD sys-tem. These outputs are automatically archived and linked into our CI/CD pipeline, giving developers immediate visibility into failures and the precise context needed to diagnose issues.

Our CI/CD orchestration, managed by Bamboo, triggers this entire process on every commit. Pull requests are gated on a clean test pass. Any failure blocks the merge and instantly alerts the team via linked PR comments and Slack notifica-tions. We also capture execution times and error rates as metrics, ensuring that core workflows remain performant and reliable under normal operating condi-tions.

Finally, every test runs in a isolated Docker container on our Ubuntu test servers. By spinning each test case up from a predefined image and tearing it down after-ward, we eliminate environment drift, minimize setup overhead, and keep our feedback loop both fast.

## Summary

Building on the testing framework requirements we defined with stakehold-ers in Chapter 3, this chapter discuss our tools selection and architecture de-cision.

We evaluated five leading E2E tools Cypress, Selenium, Puppeteer, Night-watch, and Playwright against must-have features like running custom Ja-vaScript, supporting our custom Chromium build, simulating clicks reliably, waiting for dynamic content, and fitting into our CI/CD flow. Playwright turned out to be the best selection thanks to its built-in auto-waiting, cross-browser coverage, and easy tracing.

With the selected tools and the essential requirement for testing frame-work we defined with stakeholders, we sketch our architecture: every Bitbucket push fires a Bamboo job that checks out the exact commit, spins up Docker containers pre-loaded with Node.js, Playwright and browser engines, runs tests in parallel agents, then pushes interactive HTML reports, JUnit XML, JSON artifacts and concise console logs back into the pull request and notify Slack channel. Our report and test run output is carefully defined with for-mats and performance metrics, so developers get rapid, actionable in-sights into regressions and system health.

# Implementation

## Server

All of our Playwright agents run on the same Ubuntu VM under Bamboo's Docker runner. That host specs:

- 2-vCPU,
- 4 GB-RAM Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL instance
- KVM virtualized.

We currently run up to four parallel containers (one per Bamboo plan) against that single host. Under full load, our metrics show CPU spikes up to 80 percent and memory usage topping out around 3 GB across all agents.

Disk I/O stays low, since most artifacts are written over the network to Bamboo's shared storage.

## Implementation

We implemented two core end-to-end workflows to validate HMI function-ality: a pagination test that navigates a data table and confirms both the UI update and underlying API response, and a setpoint test that opens a modal dialog, submits a new value, and verifies the change in the interface and configuration API. Each step is wrapped in Playwright's test.step(), generat-ing clear action-verification pairs in our HTML reports and capturing net-work traces for deeper assertion.

Over a two-week window encompassing 45 commit-triggered runs, we col-lected timing and stability metrics. Let 𝑇𝑖 be the total duration of run 𝑖. The mean execution time

T = <sup>1</sup>

45

45

i=1

∑

Ti = 275 seconds

with a minimum of 240 seconds and a maximum of 350 seconds. The aver-age durations for the individual scenarios were 10 seconds (pagination) and 20 seconds (setpoint). In early deployments we observed longer test run total duration due to a cold-start penalty the first time the original Docker image was pulled and built up, which took up to 350 seconds in total. This means that in our current setup, nearly eighty percent of the total runtime is con-sumed by environmental overhead. To drive that overhead down, we are ex-periencing layering browser binaries and core dependencies into base image so that only application code changes invalidate the Docker cache. Multi-stage builds further isolate infrequently changing components, like operating

system packages, from test code, meaning rebuilds only recompile what is necessary. In parallel, we are also trying a pool of always-running containers orchestrated via Kubernetes, which would eliminate image-pull and setup time altogether and deliver consistently fast feedback on every commit.

We quantify flakiness as the proportion of tests that only pass after a retry. Formally:

𝐹𝑙𝑎𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑒𝑠𝑠 𝑅𝑎𝑡𝑒 (𝐹𝑅) = Nentry−pass x 100%

Ntotal−runs

where Nretry-pass is the number of test executions that failed on the first at-tempt but succeeded on retry, and Ntotal-runs is the total number of test execu-tions.

Over our last 45 test runs we saw 2 cases that needed a second retry, so

𝐹𝑅 = 2

45

x 100% = 4.44%

yielding a flakiness rate of about 4.44 percent.

This small flakiness rate reflects the effectiveness of Playwright's built-in auto-waiting and our targeted explicit wait strategies. Allowing a single re-try raised our overall pass rate to one hundred percent.

Besides performance, our suite has significantly enhanced code coverage and developer productivity. Developers now receive test results in under five minutes after pushing changes, eliminating the median pull-request turnaround from hours to 10 minutes and saving the team hours of manual testing effort every day.

Even furthur the test result feedback quality, our Playwright test suite pro-duces three coordinated report artifacts on every run. An interactive HTML report, a JUnit-format XML, and a JSON results file, that collectively sur-face both high-level outcomes and low-level diagnostics. The HTML report offers a navigable view of each test step, complete with embedded screen-shots and trace snapshots for any failed assertions. The JSON report pro-vides a machine-readable log of every test's metadata, that we can later parse for trend analysis or integrate into external dashboards. As soon as Playwright finishes, our Bamboo plan archives all three artifacts and gener-ates a unique build URL. That URL is then injected into a comment on the

corresponding Bitbucket so that every developer sees a "View E2E report" link directly under their code changes. This linkage ensures that anyone re-viewing the PR has immediate, one-click access to both the high-level result and the full diagnostic detail without leaving their code review workflow.

In practice, we achieved a consistent one hundred percent gating of pull re-quests, no failing tests ever slipped through testing to production, while keeping test executing duration modest. Even though our current coverage spans only a small percentage of critical UI workflows, the modular infra-structure and centralized selector strategy allow us to onboard new scenar-ios rapidly. With just a few lines of configuration, we can now add tests for alarm-dialog sequencing, or any newly planned operator work flow.

Beyond these quantitative milestones, the implementation process deepened our understanding of the HMI's behaviour, uncovering undocumented API parameters, race conditions in rapid setpoint updates, which have already seeded new test scenarios and performance optimizations. This implementa-tion and the knowledge provide the foundation for the next development it-eration.

Resource monitoring on our 2 vCPU, 4 GB-RAM Ubuntu VM running four parallel Docker agents showed CPU utilization peaking at 80 percent and memory usage holding around 3 GB. Disk I/O remained minimal, as arti-facts streamed directly to Bamboo's shared storage. These measures con-firm that our existing infrastructure easily supports the current workload. However, projecting a 50 percent increase in test coverage, by adding work-flows, would push CPU utilization well beyond comfortable limits, so hori-zontal scaling via Kubernetes or additional build agents to preserve our fast feedback loop is needed.

In summary, this first implementation phase has not only validated our ar-chitectural choices but also delivered a robust framework that meets the pro-ject's goals with high effectiveness. At the same time, it establishes a clear roadmap for future enhancements.

# Discussion

Our automated testing framework has demonstrated that a require-ments-driven approach, defined in close stakeholder collaboration, can have a reliable end-to-end solution for safety-critical HMIs. By analysing the es-sential needs such as custom JavaScript execution, Chromium compatibility, reliable click simulation, dynamic-content waits, content verification, and CI/CD integration, we ensured that our solution design directly address the practical challenges faced by power-plant operators and HMI design engi-neers.

From an architectural point of view, containerizing each commit-triggered test run in Docker under Bamboo not only eliminated environment drift but also delivered reproducible and rapid feedback solution. The average end-to-end execution time of 275 seconds can provide developers with im-mediate insight into performance regressions. The measured flakiness rate of 4.4 percent, which dropped to zero with one retry, underscores the robust-ness of Playwright's synchronization mechanisms and our targeted explicit waits. These metrics show that the framework meets the demands of speed and stability required in a continuous-integration workflow.

At the same time, our evaluation confirms that our current setup, running up to four parallel containers on a 2-vCPU, 4 GB-RAM VM, comfortably sup-ports our two-scenario suite without overloading the host (peak CPU at 80 percent, memory at 3 GB). Although four parallel containers performed acceptably for our two scenarios, we cannot claim that a single host will suf-fice as the number or complexity of tests increases. However, when we ex-pand to more tests or more complex workflows, we will have to either provi-sion a more powerful server or optimize the current architecture and intro-duce elastic agent scaling to maintain performance.

Our reporting strategy, interactive HTML with trace captures, JUnit XML, and JSON artifacts, providing insight for effectively identifying failures. De-velopers could immediately navigate from a pull request to a detailed step-by-step narrative, greatly reducing mean time to resolution. However, capturing only isolated snapshots limits our ability to analyse performance drift or flakiness trends across longer periods. Integrating a historical analyt-ics platform such as Grafana or Allure would enrich our insight, enabling data-driven decisions about when to refactor tests or adjust timeouts.

Finally, aligning the framework with ISO 9241-210 and ANSI/ISA-101.01 principles validated our human-centred and safety-focused design choices while revealing areas for growth. Our tests simulate core operator workflows,

but they do not yet measure cognitive load or verify visual clarity under stress conditions. Incorporating axe-core accessibility audits and viewport-based pixel-diff checks would extend our coverage into user usability. Moreover, formalizing traceability through metadata-driven Page Objects and Zephyr integration would close the loop between requirements, test code, and failure artifacts.

Importantly, by fully automating end-to-end validation of critical operator workflows, our framework has effectively replaced what was once a labour-intensive, error-prone manual testing process. Developers now receive con-sistent, reproducible feedback on every commit, freeing QA resources to fo-cus on exploratory and usability testing rather than repetitive regression checks.

Our work answers the research questions by laying out clear requirements, demonstrating a Docker-Bamboo-Playwright architecture satisfying those needs, structuring metric outputs into actionable reports, and showing how international standards can guide future enhancements. The framework de-livers continuous feedback on every commit, significantly reducing manual effort and risk. At the same time, the discussion addresses key limitations-single-host scaling, evolving usability checks, and long-term trend analysis-that would be the direction of the next phase of development.

# Conclusion

This study goal is to identify the essential requirements for automated HMI testing, and accordingly propose an automated testing framework architec-ture, which meets the requirement of test outputs, and align with best prac-tices as well as international standards.

Stakeholder workshops defined a set of technical needs: the ability to execute custom JavaScript for internal API calls in browser context, compatibility with our customized Chromium executable, robust click simulation, reliable waiting for dynamic content, comprehensive content and translation verifi-cation, and tight CI/CD integration.

Moreover, we demonstrated that our Docker-Bamboo-Playwright architec-ture best meets these requirements. Docker containers guarantee reproduci-ble environments on every commit. Bamboo orchestrates provisioning, test execution, artifact collection, and reporting. Playwright delivers native auto-waiting and trace capture that minimize flakiness and speed test devel-opment respectively.

Our reporting outputs, interactive HTML with embedded screenshots and traces, JUnit XML, and JSON artifacts, providing developers with instant, insight into regression failures and performance metrics. These formats friendly integrate with pull-request workflows and notification channels, col-lapsing the feedback loop to minutes rather than hours.

Importantly, by benchmarking our design against field best practice, ISO 9241-210's human-centred principles and ANSI/ISA-101.01's clarity and safety guidelines, we validated our focus on operator workflows and identi-fied future enhancements such as accessibility audits, pixel-diff visual checks, and metadata-driven traceability.

In summary, our work answers the core research questions and delivers a continuous, production-grade feedback mechanism for our safety-critical HMI development process. It replaces error-prone manual regression with an automated, reliable process that scales with development velocity. At the same time, the limitations we have identified will guide future research into elastic scaling, extended scenario coverage, long-term trend and historical data analysis, deeper integration with industrial standards.

# Future work

Although our current framework delivers reliable, production-grade feed-back, there remain several opportunities to strengthen both its effectiveness.

First, we will organize recursive stakeholder feedback loops by scheduling regular review sessions with system engineers and development team. Cap-turing emerging workflows and pain points in real time will allow us to refine and add test scenarios so that our suite stays synchronized with rapid HMI development.

Second, we plan to introduce adaptive, data-driven waiting strategies and deep accessibility audits. During every run we will log actual selector resolu-tion times and calculate dynamic timeouts as the mean plus two standard deviations. When a component exceeds its historical timing profile the test will fall back on a safe maximum, minimizing flakiness and delays. In parallel we will inject axe-core contrast rules, capture full-page screenshots across multiple viewports, and perform pixel-diff comparisons against approved baselines. This will enable early detection of regressions in color contrast and layout consistency.

Our Page Object Model will evolve into a metadata-driven architecture in which each atomic module is tagged by feature area and user story. We will integrate these tags with a test-management system such as Zephyr for Jira, linking code, test definitions, and requirements in a single traceability ma-trix.

Regards of report, we will transition from standalone HTML snapshots to a historical analytics platform. By streaming test outcomes, performance met-rics, and artifact links into Prometheus and Grafana or deploying an Allure server, we can build dashboards that surface creeping flakiness, turning each test run into actionable event. We also plan to enrich our Slack and Teams notifications with contextual alerts that include metrics trends and links to relevant dashboards.

Finally, we will optimize our Docker images and test infrastructure. By run-ning cAdvisor alongside each container we can collect fine-grained telemetry. Multi-stage builds will enforce image-size budgets, while container-native or-chestration, possibly leveraging Kubernetes, will allow elastic scaling of test agents based on real-time load.

Together, these enhancements will ensure that our framework not only keeps pace with evolving HMI requirements but continues to deliver fast, meaning-ful feedback.
